title: WRAP for Your Workplace:
title_short: WRAP for Your Workplace · What does ‘not okay’ look like?
length: about 64 s (60 s of story, then a 4 s end card)
headline: WRAP makes a team better at noticing each other. A 60-second promo asking other organizations to bring WRAP to their staff.
story: Madison is good at hiding when she's struggling. Her coworkers know when she's quiet and closed off: that's not her.
WRAP lets a group name what everybody looks like when they're doing well and when they're not. A coworker without her usual morning drink gets a “hey, are you doing OK?”
WRAP made Madison a better coworker. Her ask to other organizations: bring it to your employees. Peer support doesn't come with conditions.

Loops: L1 “What does ‘not okay’ look like?” opens at 0:00 and closes on the drink story at 0:36. L2 “What does WRAP do for a team?” opens at 0:13 and closes on “a better coworker” at 0:50. Stakes: a team that notices each other before someone falls through the cracks.
do: Open on the whiteboard feelings list with the hook text on frame 1.
Show the WRAP group when she talks about the group; show coworkers when she names them.
Cut her filler (“So”, “I think”, “you know”) and pauses over 0.5 s; captions match what's left.
WRAP in capitals in every caption and card, never “rap”.
End card: “Bring WRAP to your team.” + mha-ne.org, 4 s. 60 seconds of story max.
dont: Not a sign-up video for individuals. No “register here”. Don't reuse the June sign-up promo's shots or structure.
No therapy, treatment, clinical or “facility” words on any card.
No participant face without a signed release. No minors.
No desk, keyboard or paper filler B-roll.

--- 20260909_C4587.MP4 ---
[00:00.7] All right, so first thing, Madison, can you just introduce yourself and say like your position at MHA and how long you've been working here for?
[00:08.5] Hi, my name is Madison Herman.
[00:10.3] I do marketing and employment support here at MHA as a peer support specialist.
[00:16.1] I've been here for about four years.
[00:18.3] Perfect.
[00:19.2] All right, so first question here.
[00:21.0] How did you first come across, oh, whoops, camera moved.
[00:24.1] How did you first come across MHA?
[00:27.7] I came across MHA as an intern.
[00:31.0] I had spent a lot of my life navigating mental health struggles, but I did my best to mask them.
[00:37.0] When I came to MHA, I started to realize more and more how I finally felt like I fit in somewhere and I was able to start to recognize that I had been hiding a lot of things and trying to make myself fit into these molds.
[00:53.9] I did really well in school.
[00:55.5] I was a cheerleader and at a certain point, when I was about 14 or 15, everything just started to go downhill and it just kept going downhill from there.
[01:05.8] And when I got to MHA, I was at my version of a rock bottom where I was acting on impulses and not practicing moderation and self-sabotaging a lot of the things that I had going for me.
[01:23.2] And so when I was able to come to MHA and hear people's stories, I started to realize that I wasn't as alone as I thought I was.
[01:31.5] And I actually own my mental health now instead of trying to hide it.
[01:36.7] And once I became a WRAP facilitator, I was really able to take charge of my own life and it's been pretty fulfilling for me.
[01:45.8] Amazing, awesome.
[01:46.8] Thank you for sharing your whole story like that.
[01:49.2] So next question is, what makes peer support different from traditional support?
[01:55.4] The biggest difference from traditional support to peer support for me is just not having any requirements or let me word that better.
[02:05.9] The biggest difference between traditional support and peer support is being able to be authentically myself.
[02:13.0] I don't have to show up in peer support as a perfectly healed or professional version of myself.
[02:19.5] I can just be me.
[02:21.7] And through that, I've been able to be peer supported by others and I am more open with them.
[02:28.5] I trust what they have to say more and take their suggestions a little more serious because I do know that they've actually been through what I've been through.
[02:42.8] Even in finding a counselor that has lived experience, I've realized that the different worldviews that I'm able to gain from connecting with people in peer support has made me view myself differently.
[03:00.0] It's made me appreciate all different sides of recovery, the clinical and non-clinical, because in peer support, we learn that it all works together.
[03:12.7] And I've started to kind of treat recovery like a buffet.
[03:16.1] And so trying out things that I maybe didn't like in the past and discovering that I like them now is a part of rediscovering myself again.
[03:26.8] Great answer.
[03:27.7] I like that little analogy you made there.
[03:29.1] That was really great.
[03:30.1] So tell me about a moment here or from peer support that you still think about or that stuck with you.
[03:37.7] So in my earlier days of doing employment, we did a lot of community outreach and community support.
[03:49.9] And one of the people that we were supporting was trying to get back into work after losing their family member that they had been taken care of.
[03:58.6] And we went and had lunch with them and I was shadowing an employment specialist and this person wanted to become a rockstar essentially.
[04:13.2] And us being able to go in there and say, what is your dream job?
[04:17.6] And it's not a joke.
[04:18.7] We genuinely want to know.
[04:20.8] And they took being a rockstar to how, let's look in Lincoln and see what jobs are equivalent to that.
[04:28.9] Obviously there's not a job like that on Indeed, but we found a job at a music store and she went and worked at the music store and really enjoyed it.
[04:38.5] And it was moments like that where other people laugh in your face or they think, oh, that's not possible.
[04:46.6] But what we really noticed in her was that she was trying to explain a need and the need was I wanna be around music.
[04:57.1] And so not everybody answers things that how we expect, but being able to look at that and identify, okay, how can we get as close to this as possible?
[05:09.0] I've had people say that they wanted to own their own business.
[05:13.0] And that's really hard to, as an employment specialist to start that.
[05:18.8] But then when I find a food truck that has a mentoring program, that's pretty close to, and I've met people who have gone through that mentoring program and they now do own their own businesses.
[05:35.9] And so it's not always in the moment.
[05:39.4] Sometimes I might meet with somebody and they are unemployed for six months and later on they fall off and I don't hear from them.
[05:48.1] But a couple years later, I'll be getting food from somewhere and I see them and they're like, oh, I'm doing amazing.
[05:55.3] This is my business that I own.
[05:58.5] And being able to see that person and reconnect with them and they know that, that's someone that is going to be proud of me because I never doubted them.
[06:12.3] We're so used to people telling us what we can't do.
[06:16.4] And when someone comes to me with a crazy idea, I'm able to look at them and say, okay, well, how can we make that happen?
[06:23.4] It might not be exactly how you envision it, but how can we make it as close as possible to come to fruition?
[06:31.0] And people have pointed that out to me and my coworkers that you never said any idea I had or any job that I wanted to do wasn't possible.
[06:41.8] It was just, let's figure out how we can make it possible.
[06:45.9] Awesome, great answer.
[06:47.8] All right, so what would you say to someone who doesn't believe that they can recover?
[06:53.8] I used to be one of those people that thought there were certain people that could recover and certain people that couldn't.
[07:00.0] And I think the biggest testament is just connection and talking to more people and meeting more people.
[07:09.4] The more people you meet, the more stories you hear and the more examples you see of people coming out of struggles, being resilient.
[07:22.2] And knowing that resilience exists means that it can also exist in me.
[07:28.4] It's not something that you have to be lucky to receive.
[07:35.4] I think anybody has the ability to get well, stay well and recover as long as they would want to.
[07:43.2] I know in my past, anything that I needed to change, I didn't wanna change it if other people were telling me over and over again what to do.
[07:52.1] So if you are experiencing or supporting someone that does struggle and recovery can be a lot of different things, I think it's just best to remind them that you love them no matter what and reminding people that they are worthy,
[08:12.6] whether they are in recovery or not, because that's really where it starts is to build that confidence to take that first step to recover.
[08:23.6] So true for sure.
[08:25.6] So what do people get wrong about this work?
[08:30.4] I think a big misconception about peer support and just the human services world in general is that we do this for a title or to make ourselves feel better.
[08:43.1] And I understand where that comes from.
[08:45.7] I don't want people to think that we're ever trying to fix them or that patronizing them or anything like that.
[08:54.9] I think the biggest thing to remember when it comes to that is that what the culture MHA is trying to create is that paid to be in your life or not, people don't have to experience things alone.
[09:08.9] I understand that we all wish that it would be just natural and something that would happen without it having to be a job but this is where it starts.
[09:20.2] My hope is that people that I meet and experience through MHA will eventually gain the necessary skills to branch out and make their own natural connections.
[09:32.2] And the fact that it's also able to be a job is just a bonus to it.
[09:36.9] So we really do care about the work that we do.
[09:40.4] It's not just a job to us, it really is a way of life.
[09:44.2] And that's something that the longer I work here the more I start to feel.
[09:49.9] Awesome.
[09:51.3] So if someone watching this has never heard of MHA, what should they know?
[09:57.8] I think they should know that all of our services are free and voluntary.
[10:03.6] [do not use: off-topic line removed]
[10:09.7] We really want things to be accessible for everybody.
[10:14.0] And also you don't have to be in crisis to utilize peer support.
[10:19.5] I think I spent a lot, a lot, of my life waiting to be in crisis.
[10:24.5] I had been in mental health facilities before.
[10:28.5] And so it was almost like I didn't think that I was in a crisis until I got to that point.
[10:34.2] But I didn't realize that I was just waiting, waiting for that to happen.
[10:38.3] And coming in and receiving support and going to KIA would not have been a failure, it would have been a win.
[10:46.6] And so remember that those services are available and they're free.
[10:52.6] Definitely.
[10:54.7] So how has WRAP impacted your life?
[11:00.1] WRAP has really helped me become a better human because I give myself the necessary things that I need to be successful.
[11:11.6] So it could be anything from having a good morning routine to making sure that I drink water, to making sure that I eat.
[11:19.9] These are things that when you struggle with self-care and you struggle with mental health symptoms that can sometimes fall through the cracks.
[11:27.5] And that was definitely my case is that I would always get everything done at work or with friends or family, but I would always leave myself last.
[11:36.6] And WRAP reminds me to put myself first.
[11:41.6] And that I can't be the best version of myself until I do those necessary things like meditation, getting sunlight in the morning before just sitting on my deck and spending time with my animals.
[11:58.4] Those little things are things that I can do for myself to make sure that I have a better day.
[12:03.1] And those were things that I honestly didn't do a lot of before WRAP.
[12:07.5] Yeah, that's so important for sure.
[12:09.6] So what is one thing you've learned through, you kind of talked about this already, but what is one thing you've learned through WRAP that you still use today?
[12:18.6] So a big thing that changed for me through WRAP was support.
[12:23.9] Even after taking peer support training, I was very strict on who supported me for what.
[12:30.5] And so I still had those professional boundaries, but when it came to family members or friends, I just made assumptions that this person owes me this, this person should be able to support me in this.
[12:44.3] I never asked people what they were willing to do.
[12:47.8] And I also was never open to adding coworkers or friends on my list for these very private and personal things.
[12:57.1] And through WRAP, I was able to realize that maybe it was on me and it wasn't on my supporters, because if my supporter has shown me over and over again that, hey, I'm not capable of helping you in that way, and I keep asking them for the same thing,
[13:13.2] at a certain point, it becomes on me.
[13:16.3] And I was able to look at my list of supporters and pick out really good tasks that were personal to each of them, and they were things that they offered to do, instead of me going to these people and saying, you're gonna do this, and you're gonna do this.
[13:31.3] That is not a way to live life, and I wouldn't want other people treating me like that.
[13:37.5] And when you exist in a state of not being well, that's how you start to treat the people in your life, that they constantly owe you something because you're not doing well, but that becomes exhausting, not only for you, but for your supporters.
[13:52.0] Totally, yeah, great example.
[13:54.1] So how has WRAP helped you recognize when you're struggling or need extra support?
[14:00.6] So I'm really good at hiding when I'm struggling.
[14:03.2] I'll still wake up and come to work some days, and so there's things that my coworkers and even my WRAP participants have pointed out to me.
[14:15.6] If I come to work and I'm really quiet and closed off, and I have headphones in, and I'm not trying to small talk, and my coworkers know that that's not me.
[14:27.0] When I'm at home, if I'm not super excited to walk in the door and greet my animals and excited for my night, my partner can automatically tell that there's a shift in my mood.
[14:39.0] It could even be little things like not buckling my seatbelt because I have a lack of care about my safety, or calling into work when I know that there's something important, which is just not like me.
[14:54.3] It's not that I, you know, there's a time to call into work, but on things that I'm excited about because I'm avoiding them.
[15:02.6] And so those are things that through conversation and WRAP, I've heard and I've identified, oh, that happens to me too.
[15:11.1] Oh, I also impulsively shop when I'm not doing well, and I can notice that behavior and stop it as soon as I realize that I'm about to react.
[15:24.4] Awesome.
[15:25.4] So how would you say, well, did these ones really apply to you?
[15:30.3] How does WRAP benefit your organization?
[15:32.5] [do not use: off-topic line removed]
[15:46.8] How can WRAP be beneficial to companies and organizations in the workplace?
[15:53.6] So I don't think WRAP has only made me a better daughter and partner and friend, but I know for 100% fact it has made me a better coworker.
[16:03.2] I am more approachable.
[16:05.7] I'm more reliable because I feel better about myself and my routine and my performance.
[16:15.7] If you are thinking about bringing WRAP to your organization, I highly recommend it, not only for the participants, but for your employees.
[16:24.8] It's a really good way to come together as a group and identify what everybody looks like when they're doing well and what everybody looks like when they're not well.
[16:36.4] And these are things that you start to notice in each other.
[16:39.9] One of my coworkers is a very big routine person and gets the same drink every single morning from the gas station.
[16:48.2] If I see her in the morning and she doesn't have that drink, I'm going to make a comment like, hey, are you doing OK?
[16:55.0] How are things going?
[16:56.5] If I didn't take a WRAP group with her, I wouldn't have known that because we're so used to being in our own world where we have our own routines and we don't pick up on things like that.
[17:09.3] [do not use: off-topic line removed]
[17:15.5] So being able to bring WRAP into facilities in your county or in your state is a very vital tool to finding more participants and meeting more people's needs before they transition.
[17:33.5] I think sometimes it's easy for us to forget how many people are incarcerated and how, how, OK, let me revert that.
[17:42.1] I think it's easy for us to forget how many people are incarcerated and how few programs that there are for people.
[17:50.2] And by going into these facilities and offering these wellness programs, no matter what the outcome is, we're giving people an opportunity to do something different.
[18:03.6] And that in itself is a win.
[18:06.6] And going into a WRAP group not only supports the people that are taking it, but it supports me as well.
[18:15.8] And we're able to learn about different resources and talk about those resources.
